subjects.introduction: At dawn in the village of Níyálá, with stones raining down from the mountain, Bahá’u’lláh wrapped Quddús in His own garments and sent him to safety. The gesture says much about this learned believer of Bárfurúsh, known everywhere for wisdom, knowledge and sanctity, of whom Bahá’u’lláh wrote that he differed from the Báb only in having turned toward Him. Named by the Báb among the First and the Last, Quddús wrote Tablets in Badasht that foretold a mystery soon to dawn from the horizon of Bahá, and he spoke the daring language of divine unity, though no station, however exalted, was to become a veil before the One yet to come. John the Baptist rejoiced at the voice of the bridegroom and welcomed his own decrease [1], and something of that joy marks Quddús as well: greatness shown as readiness to recognize. His life leads naturally into the circle of the Letters of the Living, toward the fearless Táhirih, and into the gathering at Badasht and its bold announcement of a new Day.
subjects.arc: Begin with an act of protection, explore Quddús’s witness and station, and end with memories of learning and identity.

order.why: Begin with Bahá’u’lláh’s protection of a threatened companion.
shortened: We were all gathered in the village of Niyala and were resting at the foot of a mountain, when, at the hour of dawn, we were suddenly awakened by the stones which the people of the neighbourhood were hurling upon us from the top of the mountain. The fierceness of their attack induced our companions to flee in terror and consternation. I clothed Quddus in my own garments and despatched him to a place of safety, where I intended to join him. When I arrived, I found that he had gone.

order.why: A reported recollection of Baha'u'llah walking with Quddus in Sari and encountering public hostility.
Locate Quddús within the relationships of an unfolding revelation.
Hear the testimony attributed to His Tablets.
shortened: And furthermore, His Holiness Quddus - exalted be His praise - hath inscribed and dispatched several Tablets whilst in the land of Badasht, which this servant hath never disclosed. Among these, They have given explicit tidings - not by way of allusion - concerning this wondrous Cause, in His words - glorified be His praise: "And when the Lord manifesteth a mystery from the horizon of Baha in His land or in one yet nearer, that resplendent Dawn from the Point of the Bayan shall have been but a herald. And when the heavens of attraction are upraised through the mystery of the mystic verses, that shall be a harbinger of Our Cause for the people of the cloud." Those blessed Tablets do now exist, and all bear witness and testimony to this Cause in the most explicit terms.

order.why: Approach the challenging language of divine claims.
shortened: For many have made claims of divinity and lordship - His Holiness Quddus, may my spirit be sacrificed for him, revealed a book on the interpretation of Samad where from beginning to end it is "I am God", and the honorable Tahirih raised "I am God" to the highest heavens in Badasht, and likewise some loved ones in Badasht, and the Blessed Beauty in the Qasidiy-i-Varqa'iyyih states: "All divinities became divine from a sprinkling of my command, and all lords became lordly from an overflow of my wisdom."

order.why: Consider the warning against allowing an honored station to become a veil.
shortened: Among what was revealed in the Bayan is the school of Him Whom God shall make manifest, and better still He says be not veiled by a Vahid of the Bayan - and the Vahid of the Bayan consists of the sacred Being and the thirteen Letters of the Living, among whom is Quddus, who according to the explicit text of the Bab has thirteen Vahids of mirrors under his shadow.

order.why: Remember learning as part of His religious life.
shortened: One of the other great and learned believers was Molla Mahomet Ali of Bar Faroosh. His title was "Excellency Ghoddoos" (Holy). He was a sheik known everywhere for his wisdom, knowledge and sanctity.
The Blessed Perfection wrote in a tablet to the Bab - "There is no difference between you and him except that he looked towards you."

order.why: A complete incident illustrating Mulla Husayn's recognition of Quddus's knowledge and the resulting reversal of their seating and service.
End with a question about His name that preserves the possibility of scribal error.
The Bab names Quddus as His companion on the pilgrimage to Hijaz and outlines the intended journey.

questions: How does the opening act of protection affect the way you read the later language of spiritual greatness?
What might distinguish recognizing a new revelation from protecting one’s established understanding of religion?
How can reverence for a person deepen inquiry without making that person a barrier to further recognition?

neighbors.invitation: Explore teaching that prepares people to recognize a truth beyond the teacher.
Consider a high station expressed through the language of servitude.

references.label: 1 · John 3:28–30 — the joy of the forerunner
references.note: John describes his joy through the friend who hears the bridegroom’s voice and welcomes the other’s increase. Compare this image with the collection’s testimony to a coming revelation. The comparison concerns the character of recognition and service, without assigning identical stations to the figures in the two traditions.

subjects.displayTitle: Jábulqá and Jábarsá: cities of expectation
subjects.introduction: Jábulqá, the city where the Imams placed the hidden Imam, cannot be found: search the whole earth for as long as God’s eternity lasts and you will not come upon it, for the earth could not contain it. The Báb does not therefore dismiss the tradition. He affirms it and draws the only conclusion left: an account that no geography can hold must be read symbolically, and so must the holy Being it concerns. Bahá’u’lláh and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá then show what literal expectation costs, as divines pronounced death sentences on anyone who doubted the two cities and a truthful man was branded a liar for centuries; Jews awaiting a hidden city of the Sabbath and Christians awaiting a descent from the clouds have the same Jábulqá and Jábarsá. The vision in Revelation of a city with twelve gates and streets of gold, lit by God Himself, asks a reader for the same interpretive labour [1]. And a dream lets the cities return, not on earth but in heaven. The question of how an image can awaken hope and yet obstruct recognition opens onto the interpretation of the Qur’án and Hadith and onto prophecy and its fulfilment.
subjects.arc: Begin with a city that cannot be located on a map, examine the consequences of literal expectation, and return to the possibilities of symbolic imagination.

order.why: Open with the argument that literal geography cannot contain the tradition.
shortened: But the Imams of the Faith have fixed His abode in the city of Jabulqa, which they have depicted in strange and marvellous signs. To interpret this city according to the literal meaning of the tradition would indeed prove impossible, nor can such a city ever be found. Wert thou to search the uttermost corners of the earth, nay probe its length and breadth for as long as God's eternity hath lasted and His sovereignty will endure, thou wouldst never find a city such as they have described, for the entirety of the earth could neither contain nor encompass it.
Since this is not in thy power, thou hast no recourse but to interpret symbolically the accounts and traditions that have been reported from these luminous souls.

order.why: Learn the features attributed to the expected cities.
shortened: For instance, the Shi'ites await a promised one who is invisible; they believe that he is the Imam Mihdi, who with servants and soldiers are abiding in Jabulqa and Jabulsa, two imaginary cities of the East and the West. Each of these cities has twelve gates. The Imam Mihdi spends six months of the year in either city.

order.why: Locate the image within a dispute over recognition.
shortened: And this group known as Babis say that His Holiness has appeared, while a faction among the Islamic sects who consider themselves Shi'ih deny this Manifestation and say that He must appear from the imaginary Jabulqa and Jabulsa - which are names of two cities - with fabricated signs.

order.why: Compare different religious forms of spatial expectation.
shortened: Jews have been anticipating the appearance of the Promised One from the City of the Sabbath which is concealed from the eyes; the same is Jabulqa. The community of Jesus [Christians] await the appearance of the Promised One from the centre of the sky, upon a cloud, descending from the most elevated zenith; the same is Jabarsa.

order.why: Consider what happens when an interpretation is enforced through threats.
shortened: Even as the divines of Iran from the inception of Islam until now maintain that the Promised One dwells in Jabulqa and Jabulsa, and whosoever speaks otherwise, they pronounce his death sentence and mock the Sunnis, since those souls do not cling to such invented fancies but rather affirm and proclaim His birth.

order.why: Contrasts searching for the Promised One in imaginary cities with His actual appearance and birth in Shiraz.
Attend to the harm of inherited accusations.
See the image reused in another contested claim.
shortened: Hadi Dawlatabadi is occupied with leading the poor people astray. He is among those who have contrived a Holy Land and a Jabulqa and Jabulsa. A whole world of idle fancies and a realm of vain imaginings hath newly appeared.

order.why: Pause over the figurative sources of honey and sweetness.
End with a dream that restores the cities to a heavenly register.

questions: What clues within a religious image invite a symbolic reading?
How can a cherished expectation become a reason for missing the reality it was meant to prepare us to recognize?
What distinguishes a fruitful imaginative interpretation from an explanation that cannot be questioned?
How does the closing dream alter the meaning of a city described elsewhere as imaginary?

neighbors.invitation: Consider the responsibility involved in interpreting an inherited symbolic statement.
Explore another use of spatial form to express religious meaning.

references.label: 1 · Revelation 21:9–23 — the city shown in a vision
references.note: The holy city is introduced through the image of a bride and described through gates, measurements, precious materials, and divine illumination. Compare the work these images ask of a reader with the argument about Jábulqá. This invites comparison of interpretive questions, without prescribing a single reading for the Christian vision.

subjects.displayTitle: The Shaykhí teachers and the work of preparation
subjects.introduction: Do you not wish for me to depart, Siyyid Káẓim kept asking his students near the end, so that the Truth may be made manifest? Bahá’u’lláh honours him and Shaykh Aḥmad as the two souls after the Imáms who grasped the inner meaning of the divine Books, and says they framed their teaching to draw receptive hearts toward a recognition they would not live to see. The subject is what a teacher’s success looks like when it means the student walks on past the teacher’s door. John’s two disciples, hearing their master name Jesus, leave him to follow and are told to come and see [1]; the Shaykhí school faced the same crossing, and not all made it. Some demanded certainty and found it a veil, some clung to a symbolic saying its author had declined to explain, some let scholarship harden into pride; and Bahá’u’lláh, noting copying errors in a text attributed to the Shaykh, models a reading that is reverent without being credulous. From here the road leads back into Islam and to Muḥammad, whose promised Qá’im the whole school was awaiting.
subjects.arc: Begin with the purpose of the teachers’ work, follow its human connections, and examine the difference between inherited learning and responsive understanding.

order.why: Discusses the relationship between Shaykhi belief, Ahmad and Kazim, and acknowledgment of the Bab.
Open with teaching directed toward the recognition of truth.
shortened: Once these blessed words issued forth from the Source of divine wisdom: "O servant in attendance! Ahmad and Kazim were aware and informed of the meanings of the divine Books. With the intention of attracting hearts, they made certain statements, and their purpose was to bring people near, that they might attain the Word of Truth - as indeed those souls who first entered the divine Law were of that party. That party it was, and this fact beareth witness to their awareness, knowledge, wisdom and the straight path to which they held fast. Well is it with them.

order.why: Notice the patient study through which teachings were transmitted.
shortened: Ismu'llah had memorized a great number of Islamic traditions and had mastered the teachings of Shaykh Ahmad and Siyyid Kazim.

order.why: Places opposition to Shaykh Ahmad and Siyyid Kazim in the historical setting of the early Babi movement.

sourceQuestion.text: Question: Can you provide an account of Tahirih's deliverance from Qazvin, her arrival in Tihran, her departure for Badasht, and the events that transpired there?

order.why: Keep a practical act of correspondence within the history.
Hear the honor given to the two teachers.
shortened: After the Seal of the Prophets - may the life of all else be sacrificed for His sake - and the holy Imams, only two souls attained unto the truth and were adorned with the ornament of true understanding: the late Shaykh and Siyyid - upon them be the Most Glorious Glory of God.
Through the nobility of these two souls, receptive souls turned toward the direction of Shin and attained unto the dawning-place of bounty and the day-spring of knowledge.

order.why: Encounter a direct address to an exponent of the school.
Examine the tension between certainty and conjecture.
shortened: The Shaykhis, contrary to the Shi'ites, believe that relying on conjecture in matters of faith is forbidden - one must act on certainty, as mentioned in many parts of the Qur'an. One day this person mentioned that he had written a thousand verses about this matter. During an argument, he stated that he believed in the Bab. When asked if he was firm in this belief, he said he had conjecture about it, and they immediately confounded him...

order.why: Ask what responsibility attaches to an unexplained statement.
Consider a symbolic prediction interpreted retrospectively.
Read the distinction between substance and inherited forms.
shortened: Answer: Know that in the latter days the Shi'ihs of Persia had forgotten the truth of the religion of God and had become entirely devoid and deprived of the morals of the spiritually minded. They were cleaving to empty husks and remained entirely heedless of the pith and substance. They had nothing to show but outward observances, such as prayer, fasting, pilgrimage, almsgiving, and the commemoration of the blessed Imams. The people of true knowledge would therefore call them "Qishri" (superficial), for amongst them the inner truths and meanings were absent, spiritual perceptions were non-existent, and heavenly morals had become but an idle matter.

order.why: Hear the Báb distinguish His Cause from a continuation of a school.
Return to the acknowledged difficulty of interpretation.
shortened: The Shaykhis themselves have mentioned that when the departed and honored Haji Siyyid Kazim - upon him be the Glory of God - was asked about the elevated one, no answer was forthcoming, and likewise from other Shaykhis. And all acknowledged that were the meaning of these passages to become manifest, they would turn towards the Supreme Horizon.

order.why: End with an extended explanation that also identifies copying errors and pride.
shortened: As to the matter of statements attributed to Shaykh Ahmad-i-Ahsa'i, upon him be all the Most Glorious Glory of God: the original statements were written by one of the Shaykhi school who inquired about them in Iraq. Several errors were observed therein, but no attention was paid to correcting them. The statements were copied exactly as written by the scribe, as is also referenced in the Tablet to Mir Karim Khan.

The Shaykh's intent was that what was created in six days has passed and ended with the Alif standing between the two letters, and in another six days that which was raised before will be raised again. Then all matters will be transformed as thou hast seen and known. Thus was the matter completed through the Proof, and the Most Great Name appeared among creation.

questions: What might faithful learning require when a teacher points beyond the limits of an established school?
How can the desire for certainty support inquiry, and how might it prevent recognition?
What does the acknowledgment of copying errors contribute to the way we read symbolic statements?
How can a community honor its intellectual inheritance while remaining open to correction and new understanding?

neighbors.invitation: Consider why an honored religious station must not become a veil.
Compare differing formulations of the relation between faith, action, and conjecture.

references.label: 1 · John 1:35–39 — a teacher whose witness leads onward
references.note: Two disciples hear John identify Jesus and then follow Him; their next step becomes an invitation to come and see. Compare this movement with the preparation attributed to the Shaykhí teachers. How does teaching change when success includes the learner’s readiness for an encounter the teacher does not possess or control?

subjects.displayTitle: Sacred forms: circles, temples, and remembrance
subjects.introduction: In the Writings of the Báb, words do not only speak; they take shape. A circle becomes the sphere through which the heavens turn, a single letter, Há, sets all the letters of creation shining, and divine names are written out as temples, as a square within a triangle, as nineteen invocations carried close. The care is exacting: white paper, seven circles of equal width, ink of gold or saffron, musk and a touch of red for permanence, and recitation after ablutions, facing the Qiblih with a heart detached from all else. In the days of Bahá’u’lláh, da’iras in the hand of Mírzá Áqá Ján were still sent to the friends for their protection. Deuteronomy, too, asks that sacred words be held in the heart and bound upon the hand and the doorpost [1]. Behind every such form lies a conviction that language and reality are woven together, and the path leads on into the meanings of letters and numbers, the art of jafr, the wider world of symbolism, and prayers for protection.
subjects.arc: Begin with a cosmic image of the circle, approach the relation between letters and creation, and then consider the care given to written forms.

order.why: Attend to the precision of a particular circular inscription.
Open with the circle as an image of divine command.
Connect a revealed letter with the appearance of creation.
Encounter the Temple through an arrangement of shapes.
shortened: O my God! Thou hast sent forth the honored Temple and the Greatest Talisman in the form of the square within the shape of the triangle.

order.why: Consider divine names written in the form of temples.
shortened: And ye shall write the temple of Unity and preserve it as ye desire. All of these are eleven units from the Names which ye write in nineteen temples, and whatsoever ye desire to add.

order.why: Read preservation together with humility and inward attention.
Explore the joining of invocation, number, and a carried inscription.
Notice the practical materials and permanence of writing.
shortened: Concerning the mystic da'ira you mentioned, the written text has been sent to your presence. As far as possible, it should be written with musk and saffron. This servant has also added some red ink for its color and permanence.

order.why: Gives practical instructions for delivering a Haykal and obtaining a transcript when fair copies are unavailable.
Place the form within an exchange between people.
Explains the distinction between the forms of letters and the numerical values studied through talismans, within a proposed order of learning.
End with a statement about continuity and fulfillment across revelations.
shortened: It was previously submitted that a da'ira would be sent, the details of which are as follows: The beginning of this da'ira existed before, and at the beginning of the Manifestation of the Point of the Bayan - may the spirit of all else be sacrificed for Him - permission was granted to some to keep it with them specifically for protection and countless affairs. However, its greatest pillar remained concealed and was not completed except in this most mighty, most holy, and most wondrous Revelation.

questions: How might the visible arrangement of words affect the attention with which they are read or remembered?
What relationship do these passages establish between material care and inward disposition?
How can we distinguish an image, a particular historical instruction, and a general religious principle?
What would help prevent reverence for a form from eclipsing the meaning it carries?

neighbors.invitation: Compare a sacred spatial image with an explicit argument for symbolic interpretation.
Consider the value attributed to a manuscript through its remembered association.

references.label: 1 · Deuteronomy 6:4–9 — words in the heart, on the hand, and at the door
references.note: The passage links love of God, teaching children, ordinary daily activity, and the physical inscription of words. Compare that integration with the written forms in this collection. What might a carried or visible text contribute to remembrance, and what inward responsibilities does its presence continue to require?

subjects.introduction: Asked what would bring a seeker nearer to God, ‘Alí gave a single answer: be truthful. The figure remembered in the Writings is at once that plain and that exalted. Challenged to prove his trust in God by throwing himself from a roof, he replied that it is not for the servant to test his Lord but for the Lord to test His servant, a refusal that echoes Jesus declining to cast Himself from the pinnacle of the Temple [1]. He called himself a servant of the servants of Muhammad while being named the interpreter of the Book, the one well grounded in knowledge, whose setting aside in favour of the bare text is remembered as a wound in the history of Islam. The Báb affirms his guardianship; Bahá’u’lláh recalls that the Kharijites, lacking arguments, answered him with a sword. Truthfulness, trust without presumption, authority worn as servitude, and the difference between reasoned disagreement and violence are the questions he leaves. They lead on to the family of Muhammad and the early figures of Islam, and to the long dispute between the Imamate and the Caliphate.
subjects.arc: Begin with a practical answer about nearness to God, examine trust without presumption, and then approach questions of authority and remembrance.

order.why: Open with truthfulness as a path toward nearness.
shortened: Then the disciple went to 'Ali. 'What do you say I should do in order to please God and to become nearer to Him?' 'One thing only: be truthful.'

order.why: Distinguish trust from putting God to a test.
Hear the challenge in another transmitted account.
shortened: O son of the Prophet of God! In an authentic tradition it is recorded that someone asked His Holiness the Commander [Ali], peace be upon him: "Is God the protector of humans?" He replied "Yes." The person asked "Are you certain?" He replied "I am confident." The questioner said "Then throw yourself from the roof!"

order.why: Notice the confidence expressed before the challenge is answered.
shortened: O you who test him who is the criterion of testing!

It is related that one day His Holiness the Prince of Believers (Ali), peace be upon him, was on the edge of a roof when a stranger submitted: "O Ali, are you confident in God's protection, preservation and safeguarding?" He replied: "How could I not be, when I am the first believer in God?"

order.why: Set exalted authority beside the language of servitude.
Sets out the station of the Commander of the Faithful as the primary manifestation of Mercifulness in the Quranic dispensation.
Consider the relationship between truth and recognition.
Hear the Báb affirm recognition of ‘Alí and the Imams.
shortened: The condemnation of God be also upon whosoever imputes to me the charge of having denied the unity of God, of having repudiated the prophethood of Muhammad, the Seal of the Prophets, of having rejected the truth of any of the messengers of old, or of having refused to recognize the guardianship of Ali, the Commander of the Faithful, or of any of the imams who have succeeded him.

order.why: Examine the place of interpretation beside the written Book.
Read a devotional remembrance of succession and knowledge.
Clarifies that reverence for Ali and the holy Family does not mean regarding them as independent creators.
Enter a symbolic interpretation of a spiritual journey.
Confront the replacement of argument with violence.
Return to the lesson of trust in a further account.
Consider the preciousness attributed to a remembered manuscript.

questions: How might truthfulness reshape the desire to draw nearer to God?
What distinguishes confidence in divine protection from an attempt to force a demonstration of it?
How do the language of authority and the language of servitude illuminate one another here?
What is lost when a dispute about interpretation gives way to coercion or violence?

neighbors.invitation: Explore how a concern for personal standing can distort a spiritual relationship.
Consider protection and restraint in a scene of religious violence.

references.label: 1 · Matthew 4:5–7 — refusing to put God to a test
references.note: A promise of protection is invoked to urge Jesus to cast Himself down, and He refuses the proposed test. Compare this exchange with the accounts concerning ‘Alí. How can the refusal itself express faith, and what does it suggest about the responsible use of an assurance found in scripture?

subjects.displayTitle: Judas and the vulnerability of faithfulness
subjects.introduction: Judas Iscariot was, by ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s account, the foremost of the disciples, a man who called others to Christ before he sold Him for a few coins. His story is kept in the Writings not as a curiosity of history but as a mirror. A pure beginning does not secure the end; envy can enter through something as small as watching honour go to another; a soul can stand for years in the holy court and remain, inwardly, far away. Christ used no compulsion with him, and that freedom is part of the warning: Judas deprived himself. Trials exist, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá says, so that Peter’s sincerity and Judas’s treachery can be told apart, which is a sobering thought about what comfort leaves hidden. When Mark records the announcement of betrayal at the table, each disciple asks whether it could be himself [1], and that question is the right one to carry. From here the path leads to the life of Christ and the rejection He met, and to the Bahá’í understanding of Covenant-breaking, where the same vulnerability of faithfulness is examined in a later age.
subjects.arc: Begin with the possibility of a changed heart, examine envy and freedom, and read the later warnings as a call to vigilance about oneself.

order.why: Read the remembered event through the language of covenant.
Begin with a good beginning that does not guarantee the end.
Uses Judas as an image of the transience of opposition in contrast with the enduring Covenant.
Examine envy as a change in the direction of love.
Preserve the place of choice rather than compulsion.
shortened: Christ did not exercise compulsion regarding Judas Iscariot and His brothers, but they deprived themselves.

order.why: Distinguish physical proximity from spiritual nearness.
Consider two senses of belonging to the kingdom.
Explore what trials can disclose about motives.
shortened: Had the doors of comfort and wealth been opened to the apostles of Christ, how could the sincerity of Peter the Apostle have been distinguished from the treachery of Judas Iscariot? The virtues of the former and vices of the latter were only revealed through tests and trials. This is among the wisdom behind the appearance of tests in the human world.

order.why: Place betrayal within the small community of disciples.
shortened: Jesus Christ, through his spiritual power, taught a few in his time, through in reality there were only twelve disciples, one of whom Judas Iscariot, who betrayed him, thus leaving eleven who remained with the Master.

order.why: Explains the connection between Judas and the superstition about thirteen while rejecting the superstition.
Consider the disproportion between spiritual loss and material gain.
Hear a direct warning about the fall of an exemplar.
shortened: Remember thou that Judas Iscariot was the head of the disciples, and their example. How then his feet stumbled and he fell from the Path, so that he shed the blood of Christ!

order.why: Retain a parallel statement without merging its identity.
shortened: Remember that Judas Iscariot was the chief of the Apostles and their exemplar, yet how his feet slipped and he fell from the straight path until he participated in the blood of Christ.

order.why: Encounter the sharp language of religious allegiance.
End with the extension of the warning to pride in other settings.
shortened: A question was asked regarding the elder brother and the Master replied: In any cycle or time someone has shown pride. In the time of Christ it was Judas. In the days of the Blessed Perfection, Subhi Ezel. Now it is the head of the Nakazeen.

questions: What practices might help us notice when affection is becoming a demand for recognition or precedence?
How do outward nearness and inward faithfulness differ in these passages?
What can a trial reveal about motives that comfort leaves unexamined?
How might a story about betrayal be used for honest self-examination rather than suspicion of others?

neighbors.invitation: Consider truthfulness as a concrete discipline of nearness.
Explore the responsibilities that accompany a recognized place in a religious school.

references.label: 1 · Mark 14:17–21 — the disciples’ question at the table
references.note: When Jesus announces betrayal by one who shares the meal, the disciples ask whether the warning concerns themselves. Compare that response with the compilation’s repeated reminders of a favored disciple’s fall. What difference does it make to receive a warning first as a question about one’s own heart?

subjects.displayTitle: Civil courts and the realization of rights
subjects.introduction: Justice needs a place to stand. One Tablet welcomes a decree that every city should have a center where lawsuits are heard and the rights of the people realized, foreseeing public calm wherever such a court takes root. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá draws a firm line between private revenge and public judgment: a father may not break the hand of the one who injured his son, though society through its courts may impose a measured penalty to protect others. Yet the Writings speak just as plainly about tribunals where bribery blinds the eyes of impartiality and favoritism stops the ears, and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá once told believers awaiting a hearing not to trouble themselves, since nothing would come of it. Deuteronomy joins the appointment of judges with a stern warning that gifts blind the wise [1]. An institution can bear the name of justice and lack its substance. The question leads onward to the culture that sustains honest law, to the Western traditions of rights and order that ‘Abdu’l-Bahá admired, and to the vision of a supreme tribunal for the nations.
subjects.arc: Begin with the promise of established rights, distinguish judgment from revenge, and test institutional hope against actual failures.

order.why: Open with the public purpose of an organized court.
Distinguish private retaliation from judgment by the body politic.
Explains why courts may intervene in labor disputes affecting the common good.
A detailed account of the social costs of inconsistent judgments and interminable litigation.
Confront the corruption of impartiality.
An incident illustrating refusal of bribery and equal justice regardless of rank.
End with a particular hearing whose promise is questioned.

questions: What practices would make the realization of rights more than an institution’s stated purpose?
Why does the distinction between private revenge and public judgment matter to a community’s peace?
How can confidence in the need for courts coexist with a clear recognition that a particular proceeding may fail?

neighbors.invitation: Consider how a change in religious law complicates the recognition of an existing claim.
Explore what happens when violence replaces reasoned argument.

references.label: 1 · Deuteronomy 16:18–20 — judges and the danger of gifts
references.note: The instruction to appoint judges is followed immediately by prohibitions on partiality and accepting gifts. Compare this conjunction with the hope placed in courts and the criticism of bribery in these readings. What must accompany an institution’s creation if its stated purpose is to survive ordinary pressures?

subjects.displayTitle: Religious law and the purposes of understanding
subjects.introduction: Muḥammad gave His people laws, not only a philosophy, and the Writings honour that practicality: a religion must take shape in daily conduct or it is a set of opinions. Yet law is also where interpretation can lose its way. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá points to the Qur’anic condition on marriage, that if a man fears he cannot deal justly with several wives he must take one [1], and observes that in God’s sight the rule of one is what is acceptable, while the clergy measured justice in food, clothing, and lodging and so emptied the condition. Bahá’u’lláh asks what fruit came of lifetimes of hair-splitting on sciences that begin with words and end with words. Other questions are harder still: what becomes of a debt of wine and pork when both parties embrace Islam, and how much certainty faith requires before one acts. These reported discussions are particular voices in a long Islamic conversation, not a summary of it. They lead back into the life of Muḥammad, into Islam as a religion of law and community, and into the question of veiling, where purpose and wording are still being weighed.
subjects.arc: Begin with religion embodied in practice, examine justice as a condition of permission, and ask whether interpretation fulfills its purpose.

order.why: Open with the practical work assigned to religious law.
Consider permission and prohibition within a theological frame.
Read a reported account of gradual social change.
Examine justice as a demanding condition of permission.
Keep a contested historical interpretation in its particular setting.
Question learning whose distinctions bear no practical fruit.
Hear a specific polemical judgment as a situated statement.
Test interpretation against a difficult question of existing rights.
shortened: I relate a parable from the religious law of Islam and the law preceding it, of which you are aware and which you acknowledge. Should a Christian, in accordance with religious law and ordinance, owe a jar of wine and a piece of pork to a debtor, and later on both should become Muslims, what course should the deputies of the sacred law follow in order to redress the right of the wronged and requite the overdue debt owed to him? For in Islam, wine and pork are unlawful and have no value, and will yield no benefit to the one to whom they are due.

order.why: Preserve the Báb’s insistence on religious fidelity in its context.

shortened: Then mention was made of a person named Haji Matlab, who was one of the Shaykhi scholars and often argued with the friends... The Shaykhis, contrary to the Shi'ites, believe that relying on conjecture in matters of faith is forbidden - one must act on certainty, as mentioned in many parts of the Qur'an.
